https://www.politico.eu/article/ceuta-cr.text: BRUSSELS — The political reaction to the surge of migrants into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta laid bare how sharply Europe’s migration debate has shifted, and how it’s forcing migrant-rights groups to rethink the way they make their case. Where previous migration crises often divided European leaders between calls for solidarity and demands for tougher controls, the response to Ceuta — where more than 100 people died last month as they tried to enter — was strikingly uniform. From the far right to the center left, political leaders overwhelmingly called for stronger borders and more effective deterrence. Advertisement Advertisement “The conversation around migration and the language used to refer to migrants has changed in many EU countries, even center-left member states,” said Michele LeVoy, director of the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, a network of organizations that advocate for unauthorized migrants across Europe. In response, migrant-rights groups are changing tactics. As humanitarian appeals lose political traction, they are turning more heavily to the courts, building broader alliances and experimenting with new ways to talk about migration. “We’re trying to be stronger together by working with organizations from across civil society, working with lawyers to challenge litigation, and really showing that these policies are bad for everyone, not just migrants,” LeVoy added. From rescue to deterrence In 2013, the death of hundreds of migrants in a shipwreck off the Italian island of Lampedusa shocked the continent. Top EU officials, including then-Commission President José Manuel Barroso, traveled to the site to declare that “the European Union cannot accept that thousands of people die at its borders.” The bloc’s then-Home Affairs Commissioner Cecilia Malmström called for a “change of approach towards migration,” adding that “this restrictive approach is not sustainable and that it is now time to move towards more openness and solidarity.” Advertisement Advertisement The 2015 refugee crisis initially generated a similarly humanitarian reaction, with German Chancellor Angela Merkel calling on Europeans to welcome more than 1 million people fleeing war in Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. The European Commission sought to manage the crisis through measures including the redistribution of asylum seekers among EU countries. But that approach ran into resistance from figures like then-Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Poland’s Law and Justice party. Florian Trauner, an expert on EU migration at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel and the College of Europe, said a handful of right-wing politicians succeeded in establishing an “institutional deadlock” that halted EU efforts to integrate migrants and allowed for a “wider shift to a more restrictive, control-oriented approach to migration.” José Manuel Barroso attends a press conference at Lampedusa Airport on Oct. 9, 2013. | Tullio M. Puglia/Getty Images That evolution is visible in the EU’s response to Ceuta. Center-left figures like Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen echoed right-wing Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s call for a more robust defense of the bloc’s external borders, and twenty-two EU leaders signed onto a letter demanding a coordinated effort to “deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration.” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen likewise stressed that “control of our European borders matters.” Without mentioning the rising death toll, she instead celebrated the fact that “not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of the EU.” The far-right factor The bloc’s shift on migration has been accelerated by the rise of far-right parties and a scramble by centrist rivals to neutralize them by embracing parts of their agenda. Advertisement Advertisement “The buffer zone that once separated the democratic right from the far right has effectively disappeared,” said Estrella Galán, a European Parliament lawmaker with the far-left Left group who is the shadow rapporteur on the EU’s return regulation. As hard-line positions have gone mainstream, the far-right has started to push for further measures, including “remigration” — the removal of immigrants from Europe. “As their policies have become widely accepted, the far-right groups have moved further and further right on other issues,” said Trauner. Hungarian border police officiers patrol the Hungarian-Serbian border on Dec. 15, 2022. | Attila Kisbenedek/AFP via Getty Images The Trump administration’s approach to migration — including large-scale deportations — “has given legitimacy to European actors who have been able to reject criticism by pointing out that the world’s major international power is embracing the exact same position,” Trauner said. Helena Maleno, spokesperson for Caminando Fronteras, an NGO that defends migrants’ rights along the western Euro-African border, said her group was increasingly being targeted by the far right. “There is a total dehumanization of migrants, especially if they’re Muslims,” she said. “We have had to reinforce protection and security — from digital attacks, but also from threats to our physical safety.” Advertisement Advertisement The far right, however, argues that migrant-rights groups have not lost influence — and still have too much of it. “I wish we could speak of the failure of pro-immigration NGOs, but what happened in Ceuta proves they have not failed,” said Jorge Buxadé, a European Parliament lawmaker from Spain’s Vox party. He accused migrants’ rights groups of being “21st-century pirates” who use “hybrid warfare” to undermine Spain’s territorial integrity. A Polish border guard stands at the Polish-Belarusian border on July 21, 2025. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images “Billions of euros every year go toward funding the structure and influence of organizations whose sole interest is ensuring that immigration to Europe remains massive and uncontrolled,” he said. Change in tactics In the new climate, the humanitarian argument traditionally used by rights groups — that migrants are human beings in need of protection — no longer carries the same political weight, said LeVoy. Increasingly, NGOs have found themselves on the defensive, fighting criminal sanctions and restrictions on their activities rather than shaping the broader debate. Advertisement Advertisement That pressure is pushing migrant-rights groups to rethink where — and how — they fight. One response is to take the battle into the courts, investing resources in legal challenges to restrictive legislation, including EU rules governing returns and the criminalization of assistance to undocumented migrants. Migrant-rights groups are also seeking to broaden their alliances. In Spain, the recent push to grant legal status to hundreds of thousands of unauthorized migrants was backed by support from the country’s conservative employers’ association and the Catholic Church . Migrants from various detention centers across Italy are escorted by police upon arrival in Shëngjin, Albania on April 11, 2025. | Adnan Beci/AFP via Getty Images “It’s more important than ever to be in strong coalitions,” LeVoy said. Her group is also reaching out to local authorities, health professionals and housing organizations. LeVoy advocated for shifting the narrative on migration by focusing less on dangerous sea crossings or dramatic border surges. Instead, she argued, rights groups should highlight the much larger population of unauthorized migrants already living alongside Europeans. She likened the strategy to that of successful campaigns for marriage equality , which sought to change public perceptions by presenting LGBTQ+ people not as an abstract political constituency but as friends, colleagues and neighbors. Advertisement “Borders are really a very small part of this issue, because the overwhelming majority [of Europe’s unauthorized migrants] come in regularly,” LeVoy said. Caminando Fronteras has likewise reinforced its legal work and security measures and built transnational networks with other rights groups. But Maleno said her NGO was also staying true to its long-standing commitment to amplify the voices of families whose relatives have died or disappeared at Europe’s borders. “We will continue to work to make the public administrations listen,” she said. “Europe will one day have to account for all those deaths and disappearances.”
